source_text: Ἀνατροφαὶ γὰρ αἱ πρῶται ἐκ γενέσεως, ἦσαν ὑπὸ γονεῦσι. καὶ πάτρια ἔθη τὰ πεπλανημένα· ὧν ἡμᾶς ἐλευθερωθήσεσθαι, οὔτε ἄλλος οἶμαι προσεδόκησεν, οὔτε καὶ ἐμοὶ ἐλπίς τις ἦν παιδίῳ μὲν ὄντι καὶ ἀλόγῳ, ὑπὸ πατρὶ δὲ δεισιδαίμονι. εἶτα πατρὸς ἀποβολὴ καὶ ὀρφανία, ἣ δή μοι τάχα καὶ ἀρχὴ τῆς τοῦ ἀληθοῦς ἐπιγνώσεως ἦν. τότε γὰρ πρῶτον ἐπὶ τὸν σωτήριον καὶ ἀληθῆ μετετέθην λόγον, οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅπως, κατηναγκασμένος μᾶλλον ἤπερ ἑκών. τίς γὰρ ἐμοὶ κρίσις ἦν, ὄντι τεσσαρεσκαιδεκέτει; πλὴν ἐξ ἐκείνου πως ἐπιδημεῖν μέν μοι ὁ ἱερὸς ὅδε λόγος ἤρξατο εὐθὺς, οἷα δὴ ἄρτι πληρουμένου τοῦ κοινοῦ πάντων ἀνθρώπων λόγου, ἐπεδήμει δ᾽ ὅμως τότε πρῶτον. ὃ δὴ καὶ οὐ μικρὸν, εἰ καὶ μὴ πάλαι, νῦν γοῦν ἀναλογιζόμενος ἐγὼ, σύμβολον τίθεμαι τῆς ἱερᾶς καὶ θαυμαστῆς περὶ ἐμὲ προνοίας, τὴν συνδρομὴν ταύτην, οὕτως τοῖς ἔτεσι διηριθμημένην, ἵνα τὰ μὲν φθάνοντα πάντα τοῦδε τῆς ἡλικίας, ὅσα πλάνης ἦν ἔργα, νηπιότητι καὶ ἀλογίᾳ παραδεδομένα ᾖ. μὴ μάτην δὲ ἱερὸς παραδεδόσθαι λόγῳ, ψυχῇ οὐδέπω λογικῇ. λογικῇ δὲ ἤδη γινομένῃ, εἰ καὶ μὴ λόγου θείου, καὶ καθαροῦ, φόβου γοῦν τοῦ κατὰ τὸν λόγον τόνδε, μὴ ἔρημος ᾖ· ἀλλ᾽ ὁμοῦ ὅτε ἀνθρώπινος καὶ ὁ θεῖος ἄρξηται ἐν ἐμοὶ λόγος· ὁ μὲν, βοηθῶν, τῇ ἀλέκτῳ μὲν ἐμοὶ, οἰκείᾳ δὲ αὐτοῦ δυνάμει. ὁ δὲ, βοηθούμενος. ὃ δὴ λογιζόμενος, εὐφροσύνης ὁμοῦ καὶ δέους ἀναπίπλησί με μεγαλυνόμενον μὲν, τῇ προαγωγῇ, φοβούμενον δὲ, μή πῃ καὶ τοιούτων ἀξιωθεὶς, τοῦ τέλους ὁμοίως σφαλῶ. ἀλλὰ γὰρ οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅπως ἐνεβράδυνέ μοι τῷδε τῷ μέρει ὁ λόγος, τὴν θαυμαστὴν οἰκονομίαν πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα τόνδε ὁδοῦ διηγήσασθαι θέλων. σπεύδων δὲ ὅμως πρότερον καὶ βραχυλογούμενος ἐπὶ τάδε τὰ ἑξῆς, οὐχ ὡς εὐφημίαν ὀφειλομένην τῷ οὕτως οἰκονομήσαντι ἀποδιδοὺς, ἢ εὐχαριστίαν καὶ εὐσέβειαν. (μὴ φορτικοὶ μὲν οὕτως ὀνομάζοντες μὲν, ἄξιον δὲ λέγοντες οὐδέν·) ἀλλ᾽ ὡς διήγησιν καὶ ὁμολογίαν, ἤ τι τῶν ἐπιεικεστέρων τούτων ὀνομάτων ποιούμενος.
thought_title: Pagan childhood, his father's death, and the Word at fourteen
orientation: Gregory recalls his pagan upbringing, his father's death, and his first turn to the Word at fourteen.
pass_a_gloss: For the first upbringings (anatrophai) from birth (genesis) were under parents (goneis), and ancestral customs (patria ethe) that had gone astray (peplanemena); from which that we would be freed (eleutherothesesthai), neither did anyone else, I think, expect, nor did I have any hope, being a child and without reason (alogos), and under a superstitious (deisidaimon) father. Then came the loss (apobole) of [my] father (patros; the print abbreviates it, Latin 'patris') and orphanhood (orphania), which perhaps was for me the beginning (arche) of the knowledge (epignosis) of the truth. For then first I was transferred (metetethen) to the saving (soterios) and true Word (logos), I know not how, compelled (katenankasmenos) rather than willing (hekon). For what judgment (krisis) did I have, being fourteen years old? But from that time somehow this sacred Word began at once to sojourn with me (epidemein), just as the common reason (logos) of all men was being filled up (pleroumenou), yet it sojourned then for the first time. Which, not a small thing, if not long ago, now at least reckoning up (analogizomenos), I set down as a token (symbolon) of the sacred and wonderful providence (pronoia) concerning me: this concurrence (syndrome), so counted out in the years, so that all things preceding this age, as many as were works of error (plane), might be handed over to infancy (nepiotes) and unreason (alogia); and that the sacred Word not be handed over in vain to a soul not yet rational (logike); but, the soul now becoming rational, if not of the divine and pure Word, at least of the fear (phobos) according to this Word, it might not be empty (eremos); but at the same time as the human, the divine Word also might begin in me: the one helping with a power unspeakable (alektos) to me but its own (oikeia), the other being helped. Reckoning which, it fills me with gladness (euphrosyne) and dread (deos) together: being magnified (megalynomenon) by the advancement (proagoge), but fearing lest, having been counted worthy (axiotheis) of such things, I likewise fail (sphalo) of the end (telos). But, I know not how, my speech lingered (enebradyne) in this part, wishing to narrate the wonderful dispensation (oikonomia) of the road (hodos) toward this man; although earlier hastening and speaking briefly (brachylogoumenos) toward the things that follow; not as rendering due praise (euphemia) to the one who so arranged (oikonomesanti), or thanksgiving (eucharistia) and piety (eusebeia) (lest we be tiresome (phortikoi) so naming them yet saying nothing worthy), but as making a narrative (diegesis) and confession (homologia), or one of these more modest names.

pass_b_english: My earliest upbringing, from birth, was in my parents' hands, and in our ancestral customs, which had gone astray. No one, I think, expected that we would ever be freed from them, and I myself had no hope of it, a child still without reason and living under a superstitious father. Then I lost my father and was left an orphan; and that, perhaps, was for me the beginning of the knowledge of the truth. For it was then that I was first brought over to the saving and true Word, I do not know how, compelled rather than of my own will. What judgment, after all, could I have had at fourteen? Yet from that time this sacred Word somehow began at once to come and dwell with me, seeing that the reason common to all human beings was only then reaching its fullness in me; and yet it came then for the first time.

Now, as I reckon it up, if not long ago, then at least now, I take this coincidence, so measured out by the years, as no small sign of the sacred and wonderful providence that has watched over me. Everything before that age, all the works of error, was to be put down to infancy and want of reason; the sacred Word was not to be handed over in vain to a soul not yet able to reason; and once the soul was becoming rational, it was not to be left empty, if not of the divine and pure Word, then at least of the fear that accords with this Word. Rather, human reason and the divine Word were to begin in me together: the divine giving help, by a power I cannot express but which is its own, and the human receiving help. When I think of this, it fills me with joy and fear at once. I am lifted up by how far I have been brought forward, yet I fear that, though I have been counted worthy of such gifts, I may still fall short of the end.

But somehow my speech has lingered over this part, wanting as it does to tell the wonderful ordering of my road to this man. Even so, I am hurrying on first, and briefly, to what comes next. I do not offer it as the praise owed to the one who ordered it so, nor as thanksgiving and devotion (let us not be tiresome, giving it such names and saying nothing worthy of them), but as an account and a confession, or under some humbler name of this kind.
notes: 'Then I lost my father': the 1622 print reads patros apobole (abbreviated; Latin 'deinde est pat[ris amissio]'), confirmed on PDF p. 79 and in Koetschau 1894. Gregory plays throughout on logos as human reason and as the divine Word; 'the saving and true Word', 'this sacred Word' and 'the divine Word' are capitalized as the Word who is God; 'the reason common to all human beings' is lowercase. 'In me' after 'reaching its fullness' makes explicit what the clause implies (the boy's reason was just maturing at fourteen). 'The divine giving help ... the human receiving help': the Greek has only 'the one ... the other'; the Latin column (haec ... illa) and the sense show that the divine Word helps and human reason is helped. 'The one who ordered it so' (to houtos oikonomesanti) is left lowercase: it may be God or the guardian angel of 4.2, whom 5.3 calls the agent of this dispensation. Doubtful abbreviation expansions noted by the source reader ('arche tes tou alethous epignoseos'; 'ho hieros hode logos'; 'panta toude tes helikias') agree with the Latin ('cognoscendi veri initium'; 'ante hanc aetatem'). 'Let us not be tiresome' follows the print 'me phortikoi men houtos onomazontes men' and the Latin 'ne importuni simus sic appellantes'. Allusion left uncited: 'the fear that accords with this Word' may echo the fear of the Lord as the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7), but no wording is quoted. 'Seeing that' renders hoia de with the genitive absolute (cause, not mere timing). The opening gar, which picks up the promise at the end of 4.2 to tell a few points, is left implicit.
